strengths: Addresses a novel and timely problem: safety vulnerabilities specific to diffusion LLMs, which are fundamentally different from AR LLMs and understudied.

Provides a clear, well-organized mechanistic analysis divided into intra-step (greedy remasking bias) and inter-step (Denoising-path Dependence) dimensions, backed by illustrative probing experiments (e.g., token injection experiments in Figures 4-5, logit heatmaps in Figure 2).
The identified 'Safety-Quality trade-off' and 'Denoising-path Dependence' phenomena are interesting empirical findings that could inform future dLLM safety research beyond this specific defense.

DiffuGuard's two-stage design is well-motivated by the preceding analysis (Stochastic Annealing Remasking directly targets intra-step bias; Block-level Audit and Repair targets inter-step dependency), giving the method a principled rather than ad-hoc feel.

Extensive experimental validation across 4 dLLMs (LLaDA, Dream, MMaDA, LLaDA-1.5), 3 safety datasets, and 6 diverse jailbreak methods (including dLLM-specific attacks PAD/DIJA and general AR attacks like GCG/AutoDAN).

Includes ablation studies isolating the contribution of each module, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (α0, λ, γ), general capability/utility checks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval), and inference speed comparisons, demonstrating the method is training-free, low-overhead, and does not significantly harm utility.
Provides qualitative case studies and a detailed algorithm box, aiding reproducibility and understanding of the framework's mechanics.
weaknesses: Inconsistency between headline numbers: abstract/intro claims ASR reduction from 47.9% to 14.7%, but Table 1 shows DiffuGuard alone only reaches 27.8% (with 14.7%/17.5% reported only when combined with Self-reminder), which could be seen as slightly overselling the standalone method's performance.

The Block-level Audit mechanism relies on decomposing the jailbreak prompt into porigin and ptemplate, which is a design well-suited to in-place-prompting-style attacks (PAD, DIJA) but unclear how it generalizes to attacks without an obvious clean/template split (e.g., AutoDAN, GCG, or fully rephrased jailbreak prompts from WildJailbreak); the ablation table doesn't test this on the non in-place-prompting attacks (WildJailbreak/AutoDAN) as thoroughly.

GCG achieves 0% ASR across all models and settings even without defenses, raising questions about whether this attack is meaningful/well-transferred to dLLMs and whether its inclusion adds real evidentiary value versus being a stacked easy baseline.

No evaluation against adaptive/white-box attacks that specifically target or have knowledge of the DiffuGuard mechanism itself (e.g., an attacker aware of the SD-based audit or stochastic annealing could potentially craft prompts to evade detection), which is important given the stated partial white-box threat model.

Reliance on a single LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4o-mini) for ASR evaluation without validation against human annotation or inter-judge agreement, which is a common but non-trivial source of evaluation noise/bias in jailbreak literature.

No reported variance/repeated trials for the stochastic components (Stochastic Annealing Remasking introduces randomness, yet single-run ASR/PPL numbers are reported without confidence intervals), making it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains.

Limited theoretical justification for the specific choice of linear step-aware decay for α (Eq. 8) versus other possible schedules, and for why Repair is applied only to the first block (a design choice justified heuristically rather than empirically validated against alternatives, e.g., auditing all blocks).

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and underexplored problem: jailbreak vulnerabilities unique to diffusion LLMs' parallel/iterative generation, which is distinct from AR LLM safety literature.

The intra-step vs. inter-step decomposition is a reasonable conceptual framework, and the 'Denoising-path Dependence' phenomenon (early-token safety injection having outsized influence on final ASR) is an interesting and intuitively plausible empirical observation, supported by a staged intervention experiment (Figure 5).

The proposed defense is training-free and plug-and-play, which is practically appealing, and the two components (Stochastic Annealing Remasking, Block-level Audit and Repair) are motivated directly by the preceding analysis rather than being ad hoc.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: 4 dLLMs, 3 jailbreak-prompt datasets, 4 additional online attack algorithms, 2 baseline defenses, ablations, and hyperparameter sensitivity studies (Appendix C), plus utility/efficiency checks (MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval, generation speed).
weaknesses: Headline number inconsistency/cherry-picking: the abstract reports ASR reduced from 47.9% to 14.7%, but the main text (Sec 5.2) clarifies DIFFUGUARD alone only reduces average ASR to 27.8%; the 14.7%-level number is only achieved when stacked with the Self-reminder baseline. Presenting the combined-method number as the headline result without clear qualification is misleading about the standalone method's efficacy.

The Block-level Audit relies on decomposing an attack prompt p0 into an 'original malicious core' p_origin and an 'adversarial template' p_template, but it is never explained how this decomposition is obtained in general (especially for WildJailbreak/JBB-Behaviors prompts, which do not come with an explicit clean/template split, unlike PAD/DIJA which are constructed from AdvBench behaviors). This leaves a central mechanism underspecified and raises reproducibility/generality concerns; the ablation results (Table 2) suggest this module is effectively inert for WildJailbreak, implicitly confirming its narrow applicability.

Heavy per-model hyperparameter tuning (α0, λ, γ, extra_steps individually tuned per model in Table 6, with α0 ranging from 0.3 to 0.7) undermines the 'plug-and-play' framing; no guidance is given for how a practitioner would set these for an unseen model without extensive search, and the sensitivity analysis (Table 7/8) shows the trade-offs are non-trivial.

Weak/limited baselines: only two generic, AR-era defenses (PPL-Filter, Self-reminder) are compared against; no comparison to any dLLM-specific or more recent/stronger defense strategies, nor to simple alternatives like pure random remasking without annealing or output-filtering with a safety classifier, making it hard to assess how much of the gain is attributable to the proposed novelty vs. simple randomization.

GCG, transferred from LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, achieves 0% ASR across all models and all defenses in Table 1, suggesting the attack simply does not transfer to dLLMs at all; including it as one of six 'diverse jailbreak methods' inflates the apparent breadth of evaluation without adding real signal.

Evaluation relies solely on a single LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o-mini) for ASR with no human validation, inter-annotator agreement, or robustness check against judge biases/false negatives, which is a known source of noise in jailbreak-defense literature.

The qualitative/mechanistic analysis in Section 3.2 (Figure 2) is based on only 5 examples, which is a very small sample to support claims about 'significant internal conflict' and the layer-wise probability dynamics generalizing across jailbreak queries.

The core intra-step fix (linearly-annealed convex combination of confidence and uniform noise in the remasking score) is an incremental modification over naive random remasking, and the inter-step fix (block remask + logit suppression) is a fairly standard remask-and-regenerate trick; the technical novelty beyond the diagnostic analysis is modest.

Using perplexity under LLaMA-2-7B-hf (an AR model) as the fluency/quality proxy for dLLM-generated text is a questionable choice given architectural mismatches between AR and diffusion generation, and no justification or validation of this metric's appropriateness is provided.

strengths: Provides a novel and well-motivated dual-dimensional (intra-step and inter-step) analysis framework specifically tailored to dLLM generation dynamics, rather than simply porting AR LLM safety analysis over.

Identifies concrete, empirically validated phenomena (harmful bias in greedy low-confidence remasking, Denoising-path Dependence) with controlled experiments (e.g., random remasking control, safe/unsafe token injection at varying steps) that convincingly support the claimed mechanisms.

Proposes a training-free, plug-and-play defense (DiffuGuard) with two complementary modules directly motivated by the analysis findings, making the connection between diagnosis and solution unusually tight.
Comprehensive experiments spanning 4 dLLMs, 3 jailbreak-prompt datasets, and up to 6 attack methods (including dLLM-specific attacks PAD and DIJA), with substantial ASR reductions reported.
Evaluates side effects on general capability (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval) and inference speed, showing minimal utility/efficiency cost, which strengthens practical applicability claims.
Thorough ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (α0, λ, γ) clarify the contribution and trade-offs of each module.
Good supplementary material: detailed algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameters, prompts, and qualitative case studies aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core analysis (Section 3) and hyperparameter settings are derived primarily/exclusively from LLaDA-8B-Instruct; generalizability of the 'Denoising-path Dependence' and intra-step bias claims to other architectures (e.g., Dream, MMaDA) is assumed rather than independently re-validated with the same rigor.

Reliance on GPT-4o-mini as an LLM-as-a-Judge for ASR introduces potential judge bias/noise that is not cross-validated against human annotation or multiple judges, which could affect the reliability of the headline numbers.

GCG attack was trained on a surrogate AR model (LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct) rather than natively optimized against dLLMs, and GCG ASR is reported as 0% across the board, raising questions about whether this baseline attack is meaningful/fair for this threat model.

The Block-level Audit and Repair module requires access to the original (pre-template) malicious query porigin to compute the safety baseline, which may not be realistic in a deployment setting where only the full adversarial prompt is observed; the paper does not clearly address how porigin is obtained at inference time for real-world/unknown attacks.

Repair mechanism is only applied to the first block, which is a reasonable efficiency trade-off but may leave later-block contamination (e.g., from mid-generation drift) unaddressed, and this limitation is not deeply analyzed.

Comparisons against defense baselines are relatively limited (only PPL-Filter and Self-reminder); no comparison to more recent or stronger model-level/decoding-level defenses, or to dLLM-specific defenses if any exist, limiting the strength of relative claims.

Average ASR reduction numbers in abstract (47.9%→14.7%) vs. Section 5.2 (47.9%→27.8% for DiffuGuard alone) could be clarified earlier, as the stronger number appears to require combination with Self-reminder, which could be slightly more transparently framed in the abstract.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: safety vulnerabilities specific to diffusion LLMs, which differ fundamentally from AR LLMs due to parallel/iterative generation.

The intra-step/inter-step decomposition provides a genuinely useful analytical lens, and the identification of 'Denoising-path Dependence' (early tokens decisively shaping final safety outcome) is an interesting and well-supported empirical finding via token injection experiments (Figures 4-5).

Extensive empirical validation: 4 dLLMs, 6 jailbreak attack types, multiple safety judges (GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-Guard, human evaluation, HarmBench, StrongREJECT) showing consistent trends, which strengthens confidence in the core safety claims.

Thorough ablations (Table 2) cleanly isolate the contribution of each DiffuGuard component and show they are complementary (Stochastic Annealing for template-based attacks, Audit-and-Repair for in-place prompting attacks like PAD/DIJA).

Includes adaptive attack evaluation (multi-sampling, gradient-based, threshold-probing attacks explicitly designed to evade the proposed defense), which is a valuable robustness check often missing in defense papers.
Utility/latency preservation is empirically demonstrated (MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval accuracy, generation speed), supporting the practical 'plug-and-play' claim.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, algorithm pseudocode, and evaluation prompts provided in appendix.
weaknesses: The headline abstract claim (47.9%→14.7% ASR reduction) actually corresponds to DiffuGuard combined with an external baseline (Self-reminder) rather than DiffuGuard alone, which only achieves 47.9%→27.8% (Table 1); this framing could be seen as somewhat misleading about the standalone method's effectiveness.

The proposed defense mechanisms (confidence-randomness interpolation, representation-based deviation scoring inspired by prior refusal-direction work, logit suppression) are fairly natural combinations/adaptations of existing ideas rather than fundamentally novel techniques, limiting technical novelty.

GCG attack results are 0.00% ASR across essentially all models/conditions in Table 1 and Table 2, making the corresponding ablation uninformative and raising questions about whether the AR-trained GCG suffix transfers meaningfully to dLLMs at all.

Despite defense improvements, ASR against strong dLLM-specific attacks (PAD, DIJA) remains substantial in several settings even after applying DiffuGuard (e.g., 39–66% under adaptive attacks in Table 9, or ~52-60% for PAD without Self-reminder in Table 1), suggesting the defense is only partially effective against the most dangerous attack class it targets.

Core intra-step/inter-step analysis in the main text (Section 3) is conducted on a single model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct), with generalization to other dLLMs relegated to the appendix; this weakens the strength of claims in the main paper body.

Hyperparameters (α0, λ, γ) appear to require per-model tuning (e.g., α0=0.3 for LLaDA vs 0.7 for Dream) without a principled selection procedure, which is somewhat at odds with the 'plug-and-play' framing and may hinder practical deployment.

Comparisons are limited to two relatively simple, AR-oriented baseline defenses (PPL-Filter, Self-reminder); no comparison to more sophisticated model-level safety alignment approaches or other potential representation-based defenses is provided, making it harder to gauge DiffuGuard's relative standing.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: safety vulnerabilities specific to diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), which is a rapidly growing area with little prior safety analysis.

The decomposition into intra-step and inter-step dynamics provides an intuitive and reasonably well-motivated conceptual framework for understanding dLLM-specific vulnerabilities (greedy remasking bias and 'Denoising-path Dependence').

The empirical analysis in Section 3 (e.g., logit heatmaps, safe/unsafe token injection experiments, randomness-vs-ASR tradeoff curves) offers some interesting qualitative insight into how parallel decoding and iterative refinement affect safety, and is replicated across multiple dLLMs in the appendix.

The proposed DiffuGuard framework is training-free and plug-and-play, which is practically appealing, and the paper reports extensive experiments across 4 models, 3 datasets, 6 attack methods, multiple judges (GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-Guard, human, HarmBench, StrongREJECT), ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, and adaptive-attack robustness checks, which is a commendable breadth of evaluation.
Reasonable efficiency and utility analysis (latency, MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval, safe-query false positive rate) suggesting the defense does not catastrophically harm general capability.
weaknesses: The headline numbers are inconsistent/misleading across the paper: abstract/intro claim ASR reduction from 47.9% to 14.7%, but Table 1's standalone DiffuGuard number is 47.9%→27.8% (~20% drop), and the 14.7% figure only appears when DiffuGuard is stacked with an existing baseline (Self-reminder). This conflation overstates DiffuGuard's own contribution and is a form of cherry-picked headline reporting.

The core mechanisms are fairly simple engineering interventions (confidence-randomness mixing with linear annealing; cosine-distance thresholding on hidden states followed by remask-and-regenerate with logit suppression) with limited novelty beyond combining known ideas (random remasking, representation-based jailbreak detection à la Arditi et al., logit suppression) in a training-free pipeline tailored to dLLMs.

The Block-level Audit and Repair mechanism fundamentally assumes the attacker's prompt can be cleanly decomposed into porigin and ptemplate, which is a strong and somewhat unrealistic assumption that may not generalize to more naturalistic or adaptive jailbreak prompts where no explicit template separates malicious intent from wrapper text (e.g., WildJailbreak's organic paraphrased jailbreaks).

Despite reporting adaptive attack results, the three 'adaptive' attacks (multi-sampling, GCG targeting SD, heuristic threshold probing) are relatively weak proxies for a truly adaptive attacker with full knowledge of DiffuGuard's thresholding and remasking logic; DiffuGuard still leaves ASR at 35-85% on PAD under these adaptive settings in Table 9, which the paper frames positively but actually indicates substantial residual vulnerability under adaptation.

The Repair mechanism is only applied to the first block (as stated in Section 4.2), which seems ad hoc and could leave later-block harmful content undefended; no ablation specifically examines multi-block repair or the cost/benefit of this restriction beyond efficiency framing.

The statistical reliability of results is unclear: no confidence intervals, variance across runs, or significance testing are reported despite many close comparisons (e.g., GSM8K accuracy drops of 1-7 points, ASR differences of only a few percentage points in ablations), making it hard to assess robustness of conclusions.

The human evaluation (claimed as 'gold standard') is only conducted on 200 samples per dataset without reporting inter-annotator agreement, annotator qualifications, or evaluation protocol details, undermining confidence in this validation step.

The paper's claims of being 'the first in-depth analysis' of dLLM jailbreak mechanisms somewhat overstate novelty given concurrent related work already cited (Wen et al. 2025 DIJA, Zhang et al. 2025b PAD) which already explore similar iterative/parallel vulnerabilities; the differentiation claimed in Appendix F.3 is somewhat post-hoc and not deeply substantiated.

Threshold λ and other hyperparameters (γ, α0) appear to require per-model tuning (Table 6), raising concerns about practical deployability and whether the reported gains would transfer to new models without careful recalibration.

strengths: Provides a novel, well-motivated decomposition of dLLM safety vulnerabilities into intra-step (remasking bias) and inter-step (Denoising-path Dependence) dimensions, grounded in clear empirical evidence (logit heatmaps, token injection experiments) rather than speculation.

The proposed DiffuGuard framework directly targets the two identified vulnerabilities with complementary, well-motivated mechanisms (Stochastic Annealing Remasking and Block-level Audit and Repair), and the step-aware annealing design is a sensible way to resolve the safety-quality trade-off uncovered in the analysis.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: 4 dLLMs, 6 diverse jailbreak attacks (black-box and dLLM-specific), 3 safety datasets, ablations isolating each module's contribution, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and adaptive-attack experiments designed specifically to stress-test the defense.

Strong effort toward evaluation robustness, cross-validating ASR results with LLaMA-Guard, human annotation, HarmBench, and StrongREJECT, which substantially strengthens confidence in the reported numbers.

Demonstrates that the defense is practical: negligible inference latency overhead and minimal degradation on general capability benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval), supporting the plug-and-play claim.

Good reproducibility support, including detailed algorithm pseudocode, full hyperparameter tables, and a thorough appendix covering dataset/attack/baseline details and discussion of dLLM vs. AR safety differences.
weaknesses: Some attack baselines appear weak or not well adapted to dLLMs (e.g., GCG suffix is trained on LLaMA-3-8B and transferred, yielding 0% ASR across nearly all settings), which limits the diversity of genuinely challenging evaluated threats and may inflate the perceived robustness of the defense.

Residual ASR after applying DiffuGuard alone remains substantial for some strong attacks (e.g., ~60% for PAD on LLaDA), with the more impressive gains arising only when combined with Self-reminder; the paper could better clarify the standalone sufficiency of DiffuGuard versus its role as a complementary module.

The Block-level Audit mechanism assumes the ability to decompose an attack prompt into porigin and ptemplate components, which may not hold for all jailbreak styles (e.g., attacks without explicit template structure), raising questions about generality to attacks outside the paper's evaluated categories.

Key hyperparameters (λ, γ, α0) are tuned per model and appear sensitive to the specific attack distributions tested; while sensitivity analyses are provided, there is limited discussion of how these would be selected in a deployment setting without access to known attack types.

The paper's core techniques (randomness injection, probability suppression via logit masking) are conceptually related to known ideas in AR-LLM decoding and safety steering, and while the paper argues for dLLM-specific novelty (addressed in Appendix F.3), the degree of fundamental technical novelty versus adaptation of known ideas to a new setting could be discussed more directly in the main text rather than relegated to appendix.
